There was a post recently about someone finally switching to Linux and I had shared a tip of putting /home on it’s on drive as an LVM. This post is to go more in depth.

Partitions, Drive, and Physical Volumes

There are plenty of docs on the internet that go over best practices for partitioning your hard drive. I won’t get into them as everyones needs and priorities are different and if I were to touch each one and explain the reasons for each configuration I might as well write a fucking book. Ain’t nobody got time for that. Instead, I want to talk about your Home drive. This is where your home directory resides, every program’s user configs, save game files, documents, etc. are located. As long as you aren’t running programs as root, every file and config will be located here. If you plan on distro hopping to find what you like the best, it is ideal if your /home was separate from the rest of the OS so it won’t get over written every time you install a new distro.

Before I continue, I need to preface all this with this…

This is by no means the ideal configuration. This is only how I have my system configured. While this works best for me, it may not work best for others. Also, I am assuming that you have already done an install and are wanting to convert over to my recomendations. If you have not done an install or are doing a fresh install and will format your drive, then be sure to put /home on its own partition (or separate drive) and select the LVM option and you can skip to the bottom for how to manage it.

So, let’s say you have your system already running but you want to put your /home on its own drive. First, let’s look at your drive layout.

[~]# df -h -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs
Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/xvda1 100G 42G 58G 43% /

So, as you can see, I do not have a separate /home drive. So, let’s attach a new volume and prepare it.

[~]# lsblk
NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
xvda 202:0 0 100G 0 disk
└─xvda1 202:1 0 100G 0 part /
xvdb 202:16 0 10G 0 disk

As you can see I have a 10 GB drive attached as xvdb. This is what I will be using for my home drive.

LVM and You

LVM stands for Logical Volume Manager. What LVM allows us to do is combine and manage disks and partitions to create larger filesystems than the disks allow separately (ie. instead of have two 100GB drives you can have one 200GB LVM). There are three terms you need to familiarize yourself with.

  • pv = physical volume
  • vg = volume group
  • lv = logical volume

All commands revolve around those three terms as you will see below.

First, let us create a pv with our newly attached device.

[~]# pvcreate /dev/xvdb
 Physical volume "/dev/xvdb" successfully created.
[~]# pvdisplay
 "/dev/xvdb" is a new physical volume of "10.00 GiB"
 --- NEW Physical volume ---
 PV Name /dev/xvdb
 VG Name
 PV Size 10.00 GiB
 Allocatable NO
 PE Size 0
 Total PE 0
 Free PE 0
 Allocated PE 0
 PV UUID dMgI2B-6R2H-oniH-mZe2-jtsx-N1Qm-egbJXv

As you can see, we have assigned /dev/xvdb to be used as a pv in our LVM setup, and it was assigned a UUID. Now, we need to create a vg and put the pv in it.

[~]# vgcreate myhome /dev/xvdb
 Volume group "myhome" successfully created
[~]# vgdisplay
 --- Volume group ---
 VG Name myhome
 System ID
 Format lvm2
 Metadata Areas 1
 Metadata Sequence No 1
 VG Access read/write
 VG Status resizable
 MAX LV 0
 Cur LV 0
 Open LV 0
 Max PV 0
 Cur PV 1
 Act PV 1
 VG Size <10.00 GiB
 PE Size 4.00 MiB
 Total PE 2559
 Alloc PE / Size 0 / 0
 Free PE / Size 2559 / <10.00 GiB
 VG UUID Z4ptfv-g0Jn-9Hou-VXrL-tx03-eif6-4hO98z

To create a pv we used pvcreate, to create a vg we used vgcreate. Can you take a guess what the command is to create an lv? That’s right, lvcreate.

[~]# lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n lvhome myhome
 Logical volume "lvhome" created.
[~]# lvdisplay
 --- Logical volume ---
 LV Path /dev/myhome/lvhome
 LV Name lvhome
 VG Name myhome
 LV UUID 3MZp1A-zuSl-SW4H-ckUV-hdiX-0Xal-nit6TH
 LV Write Access read/write
 LV Creation host, time AE1A-D-LT01-V, 2018-02-16 13:48:06 -0500
 LV Status available
 # open 0
 LV Size <10.00 GiB
 Current LE 2559
 Segments 1
 Allocation inherit
 Read ahead sectors auto
 - currently set to 8192
 Block device 253:0

Now that we have a new device, we can use it like an actual device.

[~]$ mkfs.ext4 /dev/myhome/lvhome
<output supressed>
[~]$ mkdir /mnt/tmp
[~]$ mount /dev/myhome/lvhome /mnt/tmp
[~]# ls /mnt/tmp
lost+found

Now that we have the new volume mounted and ready to use, we need to copy all the data over.

[~]$ rsync -av /home/* /mnt/tmp/
<output surpressed>
[~]# df -h -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs
Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/xvda1 100G 43G 58G 43% /
/dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome 9.8G 37M 9.2G 1% /mnt/tmp

This could take a while depending on how much data you have to copy. Once done, we update the fstab file and reboot.

Now, I know what you might be seeing. The devices are slightly different. Well, not quite.

[~]# ls -l /dev/myhome/lvhome
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 Feb 16 13:51 /dev/myhome/lvhome -> ../dm-0
[~]# ls -l /dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 Feb 16 13:51 /dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome -> ../dm-0

They are both symlinks to /dev/dm-0 which is the actual device. 

[~]# cat /etc/fstab | grep -v ^#

UUID=ef6ba050-6cdc-416a-9380-c14304d0d206 / xfs defaults 0 0
/dev/myhome/lvhome /home ext4 defaults 0 0
[~]$ reboot

Once the reboot is done, you now have your home folder on its own drive that is set up as a logical volume.

To be continued in the comments with extending and disaster recovery...
Using logical volumes for your home directory

Extending the LV

What if you run out of storage and need more space? Let’s go over management.

After attaching a new drive you need to go through the same steps to create a pv.

[~]# lsblk
NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
xvda 202:0 0 100G 0 disk
└─xvda1 202:1 0 100G 0 part /
xvdb 202:16 0 10G 0 disk
└─myhome-lvhome 253:0 0 10G 0 lvm /home
xvdc 202:32 0 20G 0 disk
[~]# pvcreate /dev/xvdc
 Physical volume "/dev/xvdc" successfully created.
[~]# vgextend myhome /dev/xvdc
 Volume group "myhome" successfully extended
[~]# vgdisplay
 --- Volume group ---
 VG Name myhome
 System ID
 Format lvm2
 Metadata Areas 2
 Metadata Sequence No 3
 VG Access read/write
 VG Status resizable
 MAX LV 0
 Cur LV 1
 Open LV 1
 Max PV 0
 Cur PV 2
 Act PV 2
 VG Size 29.99 GiB
 PE Size 4.00 MiB
 Total PE 7678
 Alloc PE / Size 2559 / <10.00 GiB
 Free PE / Size 5119 / <20.00 GiB
 VG UUID Z4ptfv-g0Jn-9Hou-VXrL-tx03-eif6-4hO98z

The new command to learn here is vgextend. We ran vgextend and told it to use “myhome” and add “/dev/xvdc” to the vg. And you can see we have 20 GiB of free space. Now, we extend the lv. I will show you the before and after usage.

[~]# df -h | grep /home
/dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome 9.8G 37M 9.2G 1% /home
[~]# lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/myhome/lvhome
 Size of logical volume myhome/lvhome changed from <10.00 GiB (2559 extents) to 29.99 GiB (7678 extents).
 Logical volume myhome/lvhome successfully resized.
[~]# resize2fs /dev/myhome/lvhome
resize2fs 1.42.9 (28-Dec-2013)
Filesystem at /dev/myhome/lvhome is mounted on /home; on-line resizing required
old_desc_blocks = 2, new_desc_blocks = 4
The filesystem on /dev/myhome/lvhome is now 7862272 blocks long.

[~]# df -h | grep /home
/dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome 30G 44M 29G 1% /home

And now we have 30 GiB of storage in /home. But, now, let’s say that /dev/xvdb starts to fail and we need to replace the drive. Wat do?

Replace shit drives

[~]# pvcreate /dev/xvdd
 Physical volume "/dev/xvdd" successfully created.
[~]# vgextend myhome /dev/xvdd
 Volume group "myhome" successfully extended
[~]# pvmove /dev/xvdb /dev/xvdd
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 0.00%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 9.53%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 18.48%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 27.43%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 36.38%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 45.33%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 54.28%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 63.23%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 72.18%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 81.13%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 90.07%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 99.02%
 /dev/xvdb: Moved: 100.00%
[~]# pvs
 PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree
 /dev/xvdb myhome lvm2 a-- <10.00g <10.00g
 /dev/xvdc myhome lvm2 a-- <20.00g 0
 /dev/xvdd myhome lvm2 a-- <20.00g 10.00g
[~]# vgreduce myhome /dev/xvdb
 Removed "/dev/xvdb" from volume group "myhome"
[~]# pvremove /dev/xvdb
 Labels on physical volume "/dev/xvdb" successfully wiped.
[~]# pvs
 PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree
 /dev/xvdc myhome lvm2 a-- <20.00g 0
 /dev/xvdd myhome lvm2 a-- <20.00g 10.00g
[~]# df -h | grep /home
/dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome 30G 44M 29G 1% /home

And there we have it. We have successfully replaced the faulty drive with a new one. Also, the new disk was larger than the old one, so if we want to, we can extend that one, too.

[~]# lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/myhome/lvhome
 Size of logical volume myhome/lvhome changed from 29.99 GiB (7678 extents) to 39.99 GiB (10238 extents).
 Logical volume myhome/lvhome successfully resized.
[~]# resize2fs /dev/myhome/lvhome
resize2fs 1.42.9 (28-Dec-2013)
Filesystem at /dev/myhome/lvhome is mounted on /home; on-line resizing required
old_desc_blocks = 4, new_desc_blocks = 5
The filesystem on /dev/myhome/lvhome is now 10483712 blocks long.

[~]# df -h | grep /home
/dev/mapper/myhome-lvhome 40G 48M 38G 1% /home

By no means is this all extensive and is only an overview of how to use LVM’s in Linux. I hope this got your ‘ol almonds activated thinking about how to better set up your own system.
